assumptions: n in {32, 64, 128, 256, 512}; 3 instances per randomised family
probes = table look-ups (machine-independent cost); wall times are medians of 3 runs on a shared, loaded machine and are indicative only
families: cyclic group Z_n, anchored x+y+1, left-zero band x*y = x (needs all n generators), the first two with one corrupted entry, random magmas
falsification: H-C17-1: a family where Light's test costs more than 10/n of the exhaustive probes. H-C17-3: a wrong verdict of the randomised test.
hypothesis: H-C17-1 (bold): Light's test with a greedy generating set beats the exhaustive test by a factor >= n/10 in table probes on every input family. H-C17-3: the Rajagopalan-Schulman test with 40 rounds never errs on the benchmark (one-sided error <= (7/8)^40 per non-associative input).
methodology: Run every algorithm on every instance; record verdict, probes, time; compare with the exhaustive verdict; for random triples use a budget of n^2/16 samples to expose its failure mode on near-associative inputs.
question: How much cheaper than the exhaustive n^3 check are generator-based, anchored and randomised associativity tests, on which inputs, and with which error rates?

summary: wrong verdicts: Light 0, anchored 0, RS(40) 0, random triples (n^2/16 samples) 27
